evidence: Kew/POWO accepts Ulmus crassifolia as native to Texas.
Hays County — the project Hays County native-source list includes U. crassifolia.
USDA PLANTS-derived county native-status data explicitly marks U. crassifolia native in Comal County.
The same USDA-derived county data explicitly marks U. crassifolia native in Travis County.
target_zone_range.guardrail: Use county records explicitly carrying native status. User iNaturalist observations are useful for learner/photo coverage but are not substituted for native-range evidence.

morphology.look_here_first: Look at the calendar and the twig before the leaf: cedar elm is a fall-flowering elm with very small rough leaves; corky twig wings, when present, can continue around the leaf node.
diagnostic_traits: deciduous Texas elm; often common on limestone and clay
leaves small, generally under about 5 cm, often obovate/elliptic and bluntish
upper leaf surface dark and distinctly rough/scabrous
young twigs may develop thin corky wings continuous around nodes
flowers in late summer to fall rather than spring
small oval samara hairy over the body/edge and deeply notched at apex

confusers.separator: Both can have corky wings. Winged elm usually has persistent regular wings ending abruptly at the node, pointed leaves, and spring flowers/fruit; cedar elm wings can continue around the node and reproduction is in fall.

Both can reproduce late in the year and have small leaves, but Chinese elm has smoother/lustrous mostly singly serrate leaves and exfoliating mottled bark; cedar elm leaves are rough and its samara/calyx are hairy.
American elm has much larger strongly asymmetric leaves, no regular corky branch wings, and spring fruit.
